takeaway: SODE accelerates pointer-chasing storage reads by executing short eBPF resubmission tasks inside an emulated SSD when cores are free, otherwise returning work to the host kernel.
background: Traversing an on-disk tree requires a read, computation of the next address, and another read. Kernel-level express resubmission avoids userspace round trips, while an SSD controller is even closer to media and may eliminate PCIe and driver latency.
villain: Device processors are slow and scarce, so queuing or executing a long resubmission task there can erase proximity gains and inflate tails. The device also lacks authoritative file-offset mappings, and untrusted application code must not issue arbitrary reads or corrupt firmware.
approach: SODE sends an eBPF task and an ext4 extent-tree snapshot with a special NVMe command. It executes immediately on free device cores or reverse-offloads to XRP's in-kernel path, validates the metadata version only after the chain, parallelizes searches across filters, and enforces address ranges plus an MPK sandbox.
impact: The hybrid design shows that near-data execution is a conditional scheduling resource, not an always-faster destination. It expands computational storage from bandwidth-reduction kernels to latency-sensitive dependent I/O, under strict task-duration and locality assumptions.

evaluation.overview: BPF-KV experiments vary B+-tree depth, threads, ranges, and open-loop load; WiredTiger/YCSB A–F tests throughput, tails, cache size, skew, resubmission time, and task parallelism.
evaluation.implemented: A Linux 5.12 prototype extends NVMeVirt, XRP, ext4 metadata versioning, NVMe commands, and eBPF with four device-resubmission threads, reverse offload, optimistic extent caching, parallel filter jobs, logical-range checks, and MPK entry/exit.
evaluation.setting: A dual-NUMA Xeon Gold 6136 server dedicates one 12-core socket and 192 GB to an emulated Optane-class device. Four resubmission cores run at 1.2 GHz to approximate Cortex-A53 performance; host applications use the other socket and O_DIRECT.

results.text: For BPF-KV random lookups, SODE delivers 16.4%–38.5% more throughput than XRP across the reported multi-thread depth-3/6 cases and up to 41% across tested tree depths.
Under open-loop BPF-KV load, hybrid SODE reaches about 10.5% higher peak throughput than XRP, whereas the on-device-only variant has lower peak throughput and worse tail latency.

Across WiredTiger YCSB workloads and one to three threads, SODE improves throughput over XRP by a 5.46% geometric mean while keeping comparable 99th-percentile latency; parallel filters cut device task time from 4,403 ns to 993 ns.

limitations: The device is NVMeVirt on server CPUs, not physical computational storage, and emulates a low-latency Optane-class device rather than mainstream NAND. Tests observe no metadata mismatch, so abort/retry cost is unknown. SODE assumes read-mostly single-device files, cannot traverse RAID-spanning data, reserves four cores, sends metadata/programs per command, and relies on stronger eBPF isolation techniques not fully implemented.
phd_group_signal: The work identifies the crossover among interconnect latency, computation time, and queueing, then designs an adaptive placement policy around it. It combines storage-stack bypass, device scheduling, safe programmability, metadata consistency, and application adaptation.

claims.text: SODE executes a resubmission filter on-device only when a device core is immediately available; otherwise it completes the read to the host with a flag that invokes the in-kernel XRP path.
A resubmission chain translates offsets with a copied extent tree and releases results only if its version still matches at completion; otherwise the request aborts.
